title: hybrid-expert-serialize-strategy-long-context-latency-investigation
content:
Summary:

This note captures an investigation into an emergent p99 latency tail when serving MoE-style models under long-context workloads (~16k–32k tokens). The cluster manifests intermittent spikes tied to expert compute serialization and queuing behavior rather than pure kernel saturation. Goal: surface micro-bottlenecks, experimental evidence, and actionable mitigations that preserve throughput while reducing tail latency for production serving.

Background / Motivation:

We observed an increase in user-facing p99s for a mixed fleet running Llama-derivative and Mistral-based MoE variants after enabling 32k context support in the hosted API. Average throughput remained within expected bounds, but spikes appeared correlated with bursts of long-history requests and multi-turn chat sessions that trigger many expert hops. Existing per-request traces showed CPU/GPU idle gaps and abrupt waits at routing/dispatch points.

High-level hypothesis:

1) Expert compute is being serialized by a combination of per-GPU stream syncs and serialized dispatch paths in the runtime scheduler, creating head-of-line blocking when a small number of large-context requests flood a single GPU.
2) The kernel launch patterns (many small-ish expert kernels) are incurring overheads that dominate latency when KV cache sizes are large and memory transfers interleave with compute.

Experimental setup:

- Models tested: custom 16-expert MoE derived from Llama-3 family (base 13B), a Mistral-style 12-expert MoE (approx 14B), and a Qwen-MoE 8-expert prototype.
- Hardware: A100-80GB (pinned to single process), H100-80GB (dev staging).
- Runtime build: runtime/master (commit 7ab3f2d) with tracing enabled; also compared with kernel-fusion branch (pr 763).
- Contexts: 4k, 16k, 32k token prefixes. Mixed arrival patterns: steady stream (200 rps), bursty (100 rps base + 50 rps long-context bursts for 30s every 5m), and poisson.
- Measurement signals: end-to-end latency, per-layer kernel timelines, GPU kernel queue depth, nvprof-derived kernel durations, host-to-device memcpy timing, fine-grained tracing for router enqueue/dequeue, and scheduler queue lengths.

Key observations and measurements:

1) Serialization points identified
- Router->executor handoff shows a synchronous enqueue in the main scheduling thread during bursts. Trace: router_enqueue syscall -> schedule_block (avg block 0.8–1.6 ms). This sync moment grows linearly with number of active experts touched by the batch.
- Per-expert CUDA stream synchronization occurs before some expert kernels (legacy safety fence), adding 0.3–0.7 ms per expert when many experts are active. On 16-expert runs this stacks to ~4–9 ms additional tail latency for single requests.

2) Kernel fragmentation costs
- For long contexts, KV cache lookups cause more fragmented kernel launches (shorter runtimes). We saw mode kernel durations drop (e.g., expert matmul kernel median 50 us down to 35 us) but overhead per kernel increases (launch + scheduling overhead dominates), resulting in net worse latency for the tails.

3) Memory transfer interactions
- Large KV cache working set causes more frequent host-side staging and intermittent memcpy stalls when the allocator triggers background GC-like reclamation. These coincide with scheduling syncs and exacerbate head-of-line blocking.

4) Queue imbalance on heterogeneous hardware
- Under mixed-model fleets, the scheduler routed several long-context heavy requests to A100 nodes already running other long sequences, creating queue depth 1.7x higher than average. Routing heuristics didn't account for long-context burstiness leading to localized spikes.

Micro-bottleneck breakdown (p99-critical path):

- Router enqueue synchronous window: 0.8–1.6 ms per request during burst
- Per-expert stream fence: 0.3–0.7 ms per expert (amplifies with experts touched)
- Kernel launch overhead (many small kernels): >30–50 us per kernel overhead net of compute
- memcpy stalls during allocator pressure: 1–3 ms occasional pauses

Hypotheses validated by A/B tests:

A) Flattening synchronization: Replacing immediate stream_fence with deferred batching fence (allow multiple expert kernels to be queued before a single sync) reduced p99 by ~22% on 16k contexts (A100). This supports hypothesis that per-expert syncs are a major contributor.

B) Kernel coalescing: Using the kernel-fusion branch that fuses small expert matmuls where possible decreased number of kernel launches by 40–60% and tightened p99 by ~18% for long-context bursts on H100. Throughput unchanged.

C) Routing backpressure: Adding a short token-aware routing backoff (delay dispatch of extra long-context heavy requests by 1–2ms to allow ongoing pipelines to drain) smoothed queue depth and prevented 40% of the largest spikes at p99 but added negligible mean latency.

Root cause synthesis:

The tail behavior is not a single bug but an interaction: long-context requests expand the working set (KV cache and routing fanout), which increases number of expert kernels per request. Legacy safety fences and per-expert stream syncs cause serialization that scales with experts touched. Kernel launch overhead then becomes visible rather than masked by longer single-kernel durations. Memory allocation and occasional memcpys further align poorly with these sync points producing compounded p99 spikes.

Actionable mitigations (prioritized):

1) Immediate (shipping quick wins, low risk):
- Switch to deferred per-batch stream fences: accumulate expert launches then sync once per request (feature flag rollout). Low-code change, reduces per-expert fence cost.
- Short routing backpressure for detected long-context bursts: implement token-count heuristic in router to avoid routing many long-context bursts to same node simultaneously.

2) Medium-term (engineering effort, targeted rollout):
- Implement kernel coalescing for expert matmuls where shapes align (refactor kernel selection path to prefer fused kernels for MoE hotpaths). Follow-up PR exists (763). Test with both A100 and H100.
- Improve allocator behavior: disable synchronous background GC-like reclamation during high QPS; replace with async reclamation windows tuned by queued bytes.

3) Long-term (architectural):
- Rethink per-expert stream model: adopt a persisting-per-request execution arena or stream pool to reduce launch/sync overhead and enable more aggressive concurrent expert compute.
- Routing-aware placement: extend scheduler to be token-aware and prefer distributing active long-context requests across GPUs and racks.

Open questions / next experiments:

- How does deferred fence interact with correctness guarantees for KV cache writes? Need invariants test for correctness when multiple experts concurrently append to shared caches.
- Quantify how many experts need to be touched before serialization dominates; build regression test around this threshold.
- Validate mitigations under mixed-tenant workload (noise from non-MoE models).

Immediate follow-ups (owners & ETA):

- Arjun: feature-flag rollout of deferred per-batch fence on staging (target 2024-11-08).
- Sofia: add token-aware routing backoff prototype in router (target 2024-11-10).
- Helen: benchmark kernel-fusion PR on H100 fleet and produce trace artifacts (target 2024-11-12).
- Miguel: write correctness regression for KV cache concurrency (target 2024-11-15).

Appendix: quick notes on traces and commands used

- nvprof/ncu traces captured with --system-wide timestamps; grep for event strings: ROUTER_ENQ / EXPERT_LAUNCH / STREAM_FENCE.
- Synthetic harness: tools/bench/long_context_replay --model=moe16 --context=32768 --arrival=bursty --seed=42
- Kernel-fusion branch tested via: git checkout pr/763; make BENCH=1 && bench/runner --gpu=h100 --parallel=8

If you want the raw traces and CSVs attached to this doc, point me to a GCS prefix and I will upload the nvprof outputs and flamegraphs for the biggest spike windows.
